I was twenty-three, ink still wet on my oath, when I found the gap in the parchment sky.

The archive vault beneath the Eyrie Citadel smells of lamp-oil and old victories—thousands of vellum rolls stitched with silver wire, each duel a constellation of blotched blood and sigils. I had been sent to fetch precedent for tomorrow’s border dispute: hawk-lord versus hawk-lord, the usual chess of talons. Instead I found my mother’s name—Seraphine of the House of Owls—cut out of the record like a tumor removed with a hot knife. The edges were singed. Someone had tried to burn the hole wider.

Only one bout missing: her last. Accused of treason for claiming the Grand Marshal trafficked serpent eggs—black, veined things that hatch mid-flight and devour the rider from inside—she was beheaded before sunset. The official chronicle claimed she never even mounted. A coward’s forfeiture, no precedent needed.

I knew better. My earliest memory is the wind in her hair the day she lifted me onto her saddle; the sky was a blue drum and we were the mallets.

That night I went to the stables. My own mount, a half-tame lanneret named Cinders, clicked her beak when she smelled my rage. “Easy, girl,” I whispered, sliding the challenge scroll between her breast feathers. “Tomorrow we dine on legend.”

Grand Marshal Veydris awaited me at dawn on the Sky-Bridge, a thousand-foot spine of rock jutting from the mountain’s eye. His gryphon, Requiem, was a bruise against sunrise—wings like cathedral doors, beak crusted with yesterday’s victory shreds. The wind carried the sweet rot of the losers he kept for fodder.

Veydris smiled, teeth filed to arrowheads. “The secretarial whelp. Blood always climbs, even when you trim the vine.”

I unrolled the parchment. “By law, a missing duel may be contested by kin. I claim my mother’s forfeited sky.”

He laughed, but the heralds stepped back; precedent is hungrier than any gryphon.

We launched. Requiem shot upward, banking to gain the sun; Cinders tucked her wings and dove beneath, using my lighter weight as a plummet. The air screamed. I felt the old stories pressing on my shoulders—every duel inked in silver, every corpse that had signed the page with its own demise.

Veydris stooped, lance of bone leveled at my heart. At the last heartbeat I loosed the serpent egg I had stolen from the evidence vault—my mother’s last proof, hidden in my bodice for fifteen years. It struck his shield and cracked.

The black serpent hatched instantly, a ribbon of liquid night. It whipped around Veydris’s neck, burrowed under his helm. Requiem faltered, shrieking as his rider convulsed. I veered aside, caught the gryphon’s reins, and slit the Marshal’s saddle-girth with my secretary’s quill—steel nib sharpened on conscience.

He fell silently, swallowed by cloud. The serpent finished its meal before it hit the treeline.

Requiem hovered, riderless, blood on his beak but no master to command the kill. I offered him my gauntlet; after a breath that lasted centuries, he bent the knee.

Back in the vault I stitched the new scroll myself: Seraphine’s duel, concluded by daughter, verdict reversed. The singed edges I left untouched—proof that history can scar, yet still be read.

Tonight the archive smells of lamp-oil and fresh rain. I file the silver wire, hearing wings beat overhead like pages turning.
